reasoning: Factor out the smallest power: 5^17(1 + 5 + 25 + 125) = 5^17 x 156, and 156 = 2^2 x 3 x 13. The complete prime factorisation is therefore 5^17 x 2^2 x 3 x 13, so of the four printed divisors only 13 divides. Confirmed by direct modular arithmetic on the full integer: it is divisible by 13 and by none of 7, 9, 11.
solution: Take out the common factor: \(5^{17}+5^{18}+5^{19}+5^{20}=5^{17}\left(1+5+5^{2}+5^{3}\right)=5^{17}\times 156\). Since \(156=2^{2}\times 3\times 13\), the whole expression factorises as \(5^{17}\times 2^{2}\times 3\times 13\). Of the four numbers offered, only \(13\) appears in that factorisation, so the sum is divisible by \(13\).

reasoning: From a + b = 2c we get b - c = c - a = -(a-c), so c/(b-c) = -c/(a-c) and the sum collapses to (a-c)/(a-c) = 1. Sympy simplifies the substituted expression to exactly 1, and the numerical check a=1, b=3, c=2 gives -1 + 2 = 1. I checked the page image at 3x because the familiar variant of this identity carries b (not c) in the second numerator and would give 2, which is ALSO a printed option; the glyph is unambiguously a round 'c', distinct from the 'b' with its clear ascender in the denominator directly below, so the transcription is faithful and the printed question resolves to 1.
solution: From \(a+b=2c\) we get \(b-c=c-a\), that is \(b-c=-(a-c)\). So \(\dfrac{c}{b-c}=-\dfrac{c}{a-c}\), and the expression becomes \(\dfrac{a}{a-c}-\dfrac{c}{a-c}=\dfrac{a-c}{a-c}=1\). Checking with \(a=1,\;b=3,\;c=2\) gives \(-1+2=1\).

reasoning: Chain the substitutions: x = y^(1/a) = (z^(1/b))^(1/a) = z^(1/(ab)) = (x^(1/c))^(1/(ab)) = x^(1/(abc)). Since x is not 1, the exponents must be equal, so 1/(abc) = 1 and abc = 1.
solution: Substitute step by step: \(x=y^{1/a}=\left(z^{1/b}\right)^{1/a}=z^{1/(ab)}\), and then \(z=x^{1/c}\) gives \(x=x^{1/(abc)}\). Because \(x\ne 1\), the two exponents must agree, so \(\dfrac{1}{abc}=1\) and hence \(abc=1\).

reasoning: y^2 = xz places x, y, z in geometric progression, so write x = y/k and z = yk. The product becomes y^((b-c)+(c-a)+(a-b)) x k^((a-b)-(b-c)) = y^0 x k^(a+c-2b), and 2b = a+c makes the k-exponent zero as well. Value 1; sympy powsimp confirms.
solution: Since \(y^{2}=xz\), the numbers \(x,y,z\) are in geometric progression; write \(x=\dfrac{y}{k}\) and \(z=yk\). Then \(x^{b-c}y^{c-a}z^{a-b}=y^{(b-c)+(c-a)+(a-b)}\cdot k^{(a-b)-(b-c)}=y^{0}\cdot k^{a+c-2b}\). The condition \(2b=a+c\) makes \(a+c-2b=0\), so the value is \(k^{0}=1\).

value: The decimal expansion of an irrational number is non-terminating and non-repeating
reasoning: A rational number's expansion either terminates (1/2 = 0.5) or recurs (1/3 = 0.333...), so the two blanket claims about rationals are each refuted by an example. An irrational number can never terminate, since a terminating decimal is a fraction over a power of 10 and hence rational. The remaining statement is the standard characterisation and is true.
solution: The decimal expansion of a rational number either terminates, as with \(\tfrac12=0.5\), or recurs, as with \(\tfrac13=0.333\ldots\) — so neither blanket claim about rationals holds. An irrational number can never have a terminating expansion, because a terminating decimal is always a fraction with a power of \(10\) underneath and is therefore rational. What is always true is that an irrational number's expansion is non-terminating and non-repeating.

reasoning: If the roots are t and 1/t their product is 1. For px^2 + x + r = 0 the product of the roots is r/p, so r/p = 1 and p = r.
solution: If the roots are reciprocal, they can be written \(t\) and \(\dfrac1t\), so their product is \(1\). For \(px^{2}+x+r=0\) the product of the roots is \(\dfrac{r}{p}\), so \(\dfrac{r}{p}=1\) and therefore \(p=r\).

reasoning: Adding the equations gives 98x - 98y = 98, so x - y = 1; subtracting gives 32x + 32y = 96, so x + y = 3. Hence x = 2, y = 1 and xy = 2. Both original equations check: 65(2) - 33(1) = 97 and 33(2) - 65(1) = 1.
solution: Adding the two equations gives \(98x-98y=98\), so \(x-y=1\); subtracting them gives \(32x+32y=96\), so \(x+y=3\). Hence \(x=2\) and \(y=1\), which satisfy both original equations, and \(xy=2\).

reasoning: The first relation gives b = y(c-z)/c and the second gives x = a(z-c)/z. Writing t = c - z, we get ab + xy = aty(1/c - 1/z) = -at^2 y/(cz), and bx = (yt/c)(-at/z) = -at^2 y/(cz) as well. The two are identical, so the ratio is 1. Six random exact-fraction test cases all returned exactly 1.
solution: From \(\dfrac{b}{y}+\dfrac{z}{c}=1\) we get \(b=\dfrac{y(c-z)}{c}\), and from \(\dfrac{c}{z}+\dfrac{x}{a}=1\) we get \(x=\dfrac{a(z-c)}{z}\). Writing \(t=c-z\), these give \(ab+xy=-\dfrac{a t^{2} y}{cz}\), and \(bx=-\dfrac{a t^{2} y}{cz}\) as well. Numerator and denominator are identical, so \(\dfrac{ab+xy}{bx}=1\).

reasoning: The condition is a - 1/a = 5 and the target is a^3 - 1/a^3. Using the identity a^3 - 1/a^3 = (a - 1/a)^3 + 3(a - 1/a), this is 125 + 15 = 140. Sympy solved for both roots of a and evaluated (a^6-1)/a^3 as exactly 140 for each.
solution: The condition \(\dfrac{a^{2}-1}{a}=5\) is just \(a-\dfrac1a=5\), and the quantity asked for is \(\dfrac{a^{6}-1}{a^{3}}=a^{3}-\dfrac{1}{a^{3}}\). Using \(a^{3}-\dfrac{1}{a^{3}}=\left(a-\dfrac1a\right)^{3}+3\left(a-\dfrac1a\right)\), this equals \(5^{3}+3\times 5=125+15=140\).

reasoning: With x+y+z = 0, y+z-x = -2x, z+x-y = -2y and x+y-z = -2z, so the sum is -8(x^3+y^3+z^3). When x+y+z = 0 the identity x^3+y^3+z^3 = 3xyz applies, giving -24xyz. Sympy substitution z = -x-y factorises the expression to 24xy(x+y), which is exactly -24xyz. Option B, 3(x+y)(y+z)(z+x), evaluates to -3xyz under the same condition, so it is a distinct and wrong value.
solution: Since \(x+y+z=0\) we have \(y+z=-x\), so \(y+z-x=-2x\); likewise \(z+x-y=-2y\) and \(x+y-z=-2z\). The sum becomes \(-8\left(x^{3}+y^{3}+z^{3}\right)\), and when \(x+y+z=0\) the identity \(x^{3}+y^{3}+z^{3}=3xyz\) holds. Hence the value is \(-8\times 3xyz=-24xyz\).

reasoning: If (x+3) is a factor then x = -3 is a root: -27 + 3(9) + 4(-3) + k = -27 + 27 - 12 + k = k - 12 = 0, so k = 12.
solution: If \((x+3)\) is a factor, then \(x=-3\) makes the polynomial zero. Substituting gives \((-27)+3(9)+4(-3)+k=-27+27-12+k=k-12\). Setting this equal to \(0\) gives \(k=12\).

reasoning: 31^2 = 961 has three digits and 32^2 = 1024 has four, so 1024 is the smallest four-digit perfect square. 1000 is not a perfect square and 1089 = 33^2 is larger.
solution: The smallest four-digit number is \(1000\), and \(31^{2}=961\) has only three digits while \(32^{2}=1024\) has four. Note that \(1000\) is not a perfect square at all, and \(1089=33^{2}\) is larger. So the smallest four-digit perfect square is \(1024\).

reasoning: Evaluate 3x^3 + 4x^2 - 7 at each option: at 0 it is -7, at 1 it is 3+4-7 = 0, at 2 it is 24+16-7 = 33, at -1 it is -3+4-7 = -6. Only x = 1 gives zero.
solution: Substitute each candidate into \(3x^{3}+4x^{2}-7\). At \(x=1\) the value is \(3+4-7=0\), so \(1\) is a zero of the polynomial. The others do not vanish: \(x=0\) gives \(-7\), \(x=2\) gives \(33\), and \(x=-1\) gives \(-6\).

reasoning: Product = HCF x LCM = 21 x 3003. Writing the numbers as 21u and 21v with u, v coprime gives uv = 3003/21 = 143 = 11 x 13. The coprime factorisations of 143 are (1, 143) and (11, 13); the first gives 21 and 3003, but 21 is not GREATER than 21, so it is excluded by the stem. The second gives 231 and 273, sum 504. Exhaustive search over coprime pairs confirms 504 is the only sum meeting the 'both greater than 21' condition.
solution: For any two numbers, product \(=\) HCF \(\times\) LCM \(=21\times 3003\). Writing them as \(21u\) and \(21v\) with \(u,v\) coprime gives \(uv=\dfrac{3003}{21}=143=11\times 13\). The choice \(u=1,\;v=143\) would give \(21\) and \(3003\), but \(21\) is not greater than \(21\); so \(u=11,\;v=13\), the numbers are \(231\) and \(273\), and their sum is \(504\).

reasoning: Expanding, (alpha+1)(beta+1) = alpha*beta + (alpha+beta) + 1 = c/a - b/a + 1 = (a - b + c)/a.
solution: Expanding, \((\alpha+1)(\beta+1)=\alpha\beta+(\alpha+\beta)+1\). For \(ax^{2}+bx+c=0\) we have \(\alpha+\beta=-\dfrac{b}{a}\) and \(\alpha\beta=\dfrac{c}{a}\). So the value is \(\dfrac{c}{a}-\dfrac{b}{a}+1=\dfrac{a-b+c}{a}\).

reasoning: By the remainder theorem the remainder on dividing by (x+1) is the value at x = -1: -3 + k - 5 - 6 = k - 14. Setting k - 14 = -7 gives k = 7.
solution: By the remainder theorem, the remainder on division by \((x+1)\) is the value of the polynomial at \(x=-1\), namely \(3(-1)^{3}+k(-1)^{2}+5(-1)-6=-3+k-5-6=k-14\). Setting \(k-14=-7\) gives \(k=7\).

reasoning: Adding or subtracting cannot create a term of degree above max(p,q), so the degree is at most max(p,q). When p is not q it is exactly max(p,q); when p = q the leading terms can cancel and the degree drops arbitrarily, e.g. (x^3+x) - (x^3+1) = x-1 has degree 1. That same example refutes option A ('greater than min(p,q)'), since min = 3 there and the degree is 1, and it refutes option D. Option B is impossible for the same reason as the upper bound.
solution: Adding or subtracting cannot create a term of higher degree than either polynomial already has, so the degree is at most \(\max(p,q)\). When \(p\ne q\) it is exactly \(\max(p,q)\), but when \(p=q\) the leading terms can cancel and the degree drops — for instance \(\left(x^{3}+x\right)-\left(x^{3}+1\right)=x-1\) has degree \(1\), which is not greater than \(\min(p,q)=3\). So the correct description is that the degree is less than or equal to \(\max(p,q)\).

reasoning: With P = sqrt(5)-sqrt(3) and Q = sqrt(5)+sqrt(3), the expression is P/Q - Q/P = (P^2 - Q^2)/(PQ). Here P^2 = 8 - 2sqrt(15), Q^2 = 8 + 2sqrt(15), so P^2 - Q^2 = -4sqrt(15), and PQ = 5 - 3 = 2, giving -2sqrt(15). Sympy radsimp returns -2*sqrt(15). The sign is the discriminating detail: the first fraction is the smaller one, so the result must be negative.
solution: Write \(P=\sqrt5-\sqrt3\) and \(Q=\sqrt5+\sqrt3\); the expression is \(\dfrac{P}{Q}-\dfrac{Q}{P}=\dfrac{P^{2}-Q^{2}}{PQ}\). Here \(P^{2}=8-2\sqrt{15}\) and \(Q^{2}=8+2\sqrt{15}\), so \(P^{2}-Q^{2}=-4\sqrt{15}\), while \(PQ=5-3=2\). The value is \(\dfrac{-4\sqrt{15}}{2}=-2\sqrt{15}\), negative as expected since the first fraction is the smaller of the two.

reasoning: Put X = x^a, Y = x^b, Z = x^c. The first term is 1/(1 + Y/X + Z/X) = X/(X+Y+Z), and the other two are Y/(X+Y+Z) and Z/(X+Y+Z). The three add to 1. Numerical check with a=2, b=5, c=-3, x=7/3 returns exactly 1.
solution: Put \(X=x^{a},\;Y=x^{b},\;Z=x^{c}\). The first term becomes \(\dfrac{1}{1+\frac{Y}{X}+\frac{Z}{X}}=\dfrac{X}{X+Y+Z}\), and in the same way the other two are \(\dfrac{Y}{X+Y+Z}\) and \(\dfrac{Z}{X+Y+Z}\). Adding all three gives \(\dfrac{X+Y+Z}{X+Y+Z}=1\).

reasoning: n + n^2 = 20 gives n^2 + n - 20 = 0, which factorises as (n+5)(n-4) = 0, so n = -5 or n = 4. Both check: -5 + 25 = 20 and 4 + 16 = 20. Option D (5 or -4) fails both ways: 5 + 25 = 30 and -4 + 16 = 12.
solution: The condition is \(n+n^{2}=20\), that is \(n^{2}+n-20=0\). Factorising, \((n+5)(n-4)=0\), so \(n=-5\) or \(n=4\). Both work, since \(-5+25=20\) and \(4+16=20\).

solution: Take the original price as \(100\) and the consumption as \(1\) unit, so the budget is \(100\). After a \(25\%\) rise the price is \(125\), so the consumption that keeps the budget at \(100\) is \(\dfrac{100}{125}=0.8\) units. That is a fall of \(0.2\) from \(1\), which is a reduction of \(20\%\).

solution: Of the \(2000\) registered students, \(\dfrac{1}{25}\times 2000=80\) did not appear, so \(1920\) appeared. Of those who appeared, \(\dfrac{11}{20}\times 1920=1056\) passed. Note that \(1920\) is the number who appeared, not the number who passed.

reasoning: The overbar is the whole question. 0.999... recurring equals exactly 1 (if u = 0.999... then 10u = 9 + u, so u = 1), so the difference from the terminating 0.9 is 1 - 0.9 = 0.1. Read instead as the terminating 0.999 the answer would be 0.099, which is also a printed option, so the distinction is load-bearing; the page image at page-level zoom clearly shows the bar over the 9 of the first number and no bar on the second.
solution: The recurring decimal \(0.\overline{9}\) is exactly equal to \(1\): if \(u=0.\overline{9}\) then \(10u=9.\overline{9}=9+u\), so \(9u=9\) and \(u=1\). The second number is the terminating decimal \(0.9\). Their difference is therefore \(1-0.9=0.1\); it is the recurring bar that makes this \(0.1\) rather than \(0.099\).

reasoning: From B:C = 3:4 and C:D = 2:3, scale the second to C:D = 4:6 so that B:C:D = 3:4:6. Then D:E = 3:4 scales to D:E = 6:8, giving B:D:E = 3:6:8 and B:E = 3:8. The ratio A:B is not needed. Sympy arithmetic on the chained fractions returns 3/8.
solution: From \(B:C=3:4\) and \(C:D=2:3\), scale the second so the shared term matches: \(C:D=4:6\), giving \(B:C:D=3:4:6\). Then \(D:E=3:4\) scales to \(D:E=6:8\), so \(B:D:E=3:6:8\). Hence \(B:E=3:8\); the ratio \(A:B\) plays no part.

reasoning: The job is 10 x 12 = 120 woman-days, so one woman does 1/120 per day; it is also 5 x 8 = 40 man-days, so one man does 1/40 per day. Six women and three men together do 6/120 + 3/40 = 1/20 + 3/40 = 5/40 = 1/8 per day, so 8 days.
solution: The job takes \(10\times 12=120\) woman-days, so one woman does \(\dfrac{1}{120}\) of it per day; it also takes \(5\times 8=40\) man-days, so one man does \(\dfrac{1}{40}\) per day. Together, \(6\) women and \(3\) men complete \(\dfrac{6}{120}+\dfrac{3}{40}=\dfrac{1}{20}+\dfrac{3}{40}=\dfrac{5}{40}=\dfrac18\) of the work each day. So the whole job takes \(8\) days.

reasoning: A quarter of the work took 200 x 50 = 10000 man-days, so the whole job is 40000 man-days. The remaining three quarters is 30000 man-days to be done in the 100 days left, needing 300 men. With 200 already employed, 100 additional men are required.
solution: In \(50\) days, \(200\) men complete a quarter of the work, so a quarter needs \(200\times 50=10\,000\) man-days and the whole job needs \(40\,000\) man-days. The remaining three quarters is \(30\,000\) man-days, to be finished in the \(100\) days that are left, which needs \(\dfrac{30\,000}{100}=300\) men. Since \(200\) are already at work, \(100\) more must be employed.

reasoning: 60 km/hour = 60000/3600 = 50/3 m/s. Crossing a pole covers exactly the train's own length, so length = (50/3) x 30 = 500 m.
solution: Converting units, \(60\) km per hour is \(\dfrac{60\times 1000}{3600}=\dfrac{50}{3}\) metres per second. Crossing a pole means covering exactly the train's own length, since the pole has no length of its own. So the length is \(\dfrac{50}{3}\times 30=500\) metres.

reasoning: Let A's share be x. Then B's is x - 20 and C's is x + 20, so the total 3x = 120 and x = 40. B's share is 20. Check: 20 + 40 + 60 = 120.
solution: Let \(A\)'s share be \(x\) rupees. Then \(B\)'s share is \(x-20\) and \(C\)'s share is \(x+20\), so the total is \(3x=120\) and \(x=40\). Hence \(B\) receives \(40-20=20\) rupees, and the three shares \(20,\;40,\;60\) do add to \(120\).

reasoning: Inverse variation means the product M x N is constant. The complete first column gives 15 x (-4) = -60. Then A = -60/(-6) = 10, B = -60/2 = -30 and C = -60/60 = -1, so the ordered triple is (10, -30, -1).
solution: In inverse variation the product \(M\times N\) is constant, and the one complete column gives \(15\times(-4)=-60\). So \(A=\dfrac{-60}{-6}=10\), \(B=\dfrac{-60}{2}=-30\), and for the last column \(C=\dfrac{-60}{60}=-1\). The values in order are \(10,\;-30,\;-1\).

reasoning: He pays 5% and receives 5.5%, gaining the 0.5% difference each year on Rs 5000: 5000 x 0.005 x 2 = 50 under simple interest. Under compound interest the gain would be 5000(1.055^2 - 1.05^2) = 52.625, which matches no printed option, so simple interest is the only reading that resolves and is the standard convention here.
solution: He pays interest at \(5\%\) and receives it at \(5.5\%\), so each year he keeps the difference of \(0.5\%\) on Rs. \(5{,}000\). Over two years that is \(5000\times\dfrac{0.5}{100}\times 2=50\). His gain is Rs. \(50\).

reasoning: Average 25 for two people means their ages total 50. The son is 17 in seven years, so he is 10 now, making the father 40. After 10 years the father is 50.
solution: An average of \(25\) for two people means their present ages total \(50\). The son will be \(17\) after seven years, so he is \(17-7=10\) now, which makes the father \(50-10=40\). After \(10\) more years the father will be \(50\) years old.

reasoning: Five tractors plough 5 hectares in 5 days, so one tractor ploughs 1 hectare in 5 days, i.e. 1/5 hectare per day. The required rate is 100/50 = 2 hectares per day, needing 2 / (1/5) = 10 tractors. The trap answer 5 comes from assuming the 'all fives' pattern carries over unchanged.
solution: Five tractors plough \(5\) hectares in \(5\) days, so one tractor ploughs \(1\) hectare in \(5\) days, a rate of \(\dfrac15\) hectare per day. Ploughing \(100\) hectares in \(50\) days calls for a rate of \(\dfrac{100}{50}=2\) hectares per day. The number of tractors needed is \(\dfrac{2}{1/5}=10\).

reasoning: Gaining 25% annually multiplies the capital by 5/4 each year, so after three years it is P(5/4)^3 = 125P/64 = 10000, giving P = 10000 x 64/125 = 5120 exactly.
solution: Gaining \(25\%\) a year multiplies the capital by \(\dfrac54\) each year, so after three years it stands at \(P\times\left(\dfrac54\right)^{3}=\dfrac{125P}{64}\). Setting \(\dfrac{125P}{64}=10\,000\) gives \(P=\dfrac{10\,000\times 64}{125}=5120\). The merchant originally invested Rs. \(5{,}120\).

reasoning: The purely recurring 0.459459... equals 459/999; since 999 = 27 x 37 and 459 = 27 x 17, it reduces to 17/37, denominator 37. The terminating 0.459459459 has a power of 10 as denominator. The other two shift the recurrence: 0.0459459... = 459/9990 = 17/370 and 0.00459459... = 17/3700, neither with denominator 37.
solution: For the purely recurring decimal \(0.\overline{459}\) the value is \(\dfrac{459}{999}\). Since \(999=27\times 37\) and \(459=27\times 17\), this reduces to \(\dfrac{17}{37}\), whose denominator is \(37\). Shifting the recurrence one or two places to the right instead gives \(\dfrac{17}{370}\) and \(\dfrac{17}{3700}\), and the terminating \(0.459459459\) has a power of \(10\) underneath, so none of those qualifies.

reasoning: For 0 < m < 1 the logarithm is negative while the other three are positive, so log is smallest. Squaring a number below 1 makes it smaller, so m^2 < m, and m^(-1) = 1/m > 1 > m. Order: log < m^2 < m < 1/m. Numerically at m = 1/3: -0.477, 0.111, 0.333, 3.
solution: For \(0<m<1\) the logarithm \(\log_{10}m\) is negative, while \(m,\;m^{2}\) and \(m^{-1}\) are all positive, so the logarithm is the smallest. Squaring a number between \(0\) and \(1\) makes it smaller, so \(m^{2}<m\), and \(m^{-1}=\dfrac1m>1>m\). Hence \(\log_{10}m<m^{2}<m<m^{-1}\); with \(m=\tfrac13\) the four values are about \(-0.477,\;0.111,\;0.333\) and \(3\).

reasoning: Let the widow (the mother) receive w. Each daughter gets 2w and each son gets 3 x 2w = 6w. Total = w + 5(6w) + 4(2w) = 39w = 39000, so w = 1000.
solution: Let the widow's share be \(w\). Each daughter receives twice as much as their mother, so \(2w\), and each son receives three times a daughter's share, so \(6w\). The total is \(w+5(6w)+4(2w)=39w\), and setting \(39w=39{,}000\) gives \(w=1000\). The widow's share is Rs. \(1{,}000\).

reasoning: Let the numbers be u, v, w with uv = 286 and vw = 770. The middle number v divides both, and gcd(286, 770) = 22, so v = 22, u = 13, w = 35. These are pairwise coprime as required and sum to 70.
solution: Let the three numbers be \(u,v,w\) with \(uv=286\) and \(vw=770\). The middle number \(v\) divides both products, and \(\gcd(286,770)=22\), so \(v=22\), giving \(u=13\) and \(w=35\). These are indeed coprime in pairs, and their sum is \(13+22+35=70\).

reasoning: Let her age be 10u + v and his 10v + u with v > u. Sum = 11(u+v), difference = 9(v-u). The condition 9(v-u) = (1/11) x 11(u+v) = u+v gives 8v = 10u, i.e. 4v = 5u, so u = 4, v = 5. Ages 45 and 54, difference 9. Exhaustive search over all two-digit pairs finds this as the only solution.
solution: Let her age be \(10u+v\) and his be \(10v+u\), with \(v>u\) since he is older. Their sum is \(11(u+v)\) and their difference is \(9(v-u)\), so the condition gives \(9(v-u)=\dfrac{11(u+v)}{11}=u+v\). This reduces to \(8v=10u\), that is \(4v=5u\), so \(u=4\) and \(v=5\); the ages are \(45\) and \(54\) and the difference is \(9\) years.

reasoning: Let the speeds be P and G and the combined length L. Same direction takes L/(P-G), opposite takes L/(P+G), and the condition L/(P-G) = 3L/(P+G) gives P+G = 3(P-G), so 4G = 2P and P:G = 2:1. Sympy solve returns P = 2G.
solution: Let the speeds be \(P\) and \(G\) and the total length to be passed \(L\).
